name: named-constructor
intent: Give each distinct way of creating an object its own well-named class-level creation operation (static factory, class method or associated function) instead of relying on constructor overloading, so that construction intent is visible in the name and the creator can validate, cache, choose a subtype, or decline to create an instance at all.
problem: A type's construction API is expressed only through constructors, which cannot carry names, cannot decline to create an object, cannot return a subtype, and cannot be replaced. Several construction routes that differ in intent collide in one signature (Point(float, float) for rectangular and polar coordinates, BigInteger(int, int, Random) for probable primes), callers cannot tell what a call means, and each new route forces either an awkward flag parameter or a hierarchy of subclasses. As soon as construction also wants caching, interning, subtype selection or failure handling, a constructor is simply the wrong abstraction.
context: Applies wherever a type can be created in more than one semantically distinct way, or where creation itself must be controlled: value objects with several representations or units (coordinates, durations, money), parsing and conversion entry points that may fail, instance-controlled types (caching, interning, singletons), APIs that must hide their implementation classes or pick a representation from the arguments, and ownership-sensitive creation in C++/Rust where the creator decides value vs. heap and the smart-pointer policy. It is a type-local decision, so it applies in every paradigm - class-based, functional (smart constructors) and procedural (creator functions) alike.
benefits: Construction intent is expressible in the name: instead of overloading one constructor by argument shape, each route gets an intention-revealing operation (Point::polar vs Point::rectangular, BigInteger.probablePrime, Duration.fromSeconds, String::from_utf8).

Creation and validation live in one controlled place: every instance passes through a named operation, so invariants are enforced once at the point where the object comes into existence and half-built objects never escape.

The creator need not create a new object: cached, interned or preconstructed instances can be returned, giving instance control (canonical values, flyweights, singletons) and removing duplicate allocation for equivalent inputs.

The declared return type can be an interface or base class while the concrete class stays hidden (List.of returns private implementations, EnumSet picks RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet by cardinality, Go constructors return interfaces), so implementation classes remain free to change.

Fallible construction becomes an ordinary return value: parsing and conversion factories (Instant.parse, TryFrom, String::from_utf8, Path.of) report failure by return value or documented exception instead of a constructor that can only throw or produce a partially initialized object.

Creation policy parameters that do not belong to the type stay out of the type: unit conversions, storage strategies and ownership decisions are visible at the creation site (make_unique/make_shared, Box/Arc) and C++17 guaranteed copy elision makes a factory returning by value as cheap as a constructor.
tradeoffs: Keeping constructors non-public to force creation through the factories removes inheritance as an extension path: a type whose constructors are private cannot be subclassed (Effective Java's first listed disadvantage), so frameworks that specialize by subclassing are locked out unless a protected constructor is kept.

Factories are not discoverable the way constructors are: they sit among ordinary static methods, IDE completion and documentation generators do not lead users to them, and callers may never find how to create the type - the reason the .NET guidelines still say to prefer constructors.

Static creation is not polymorphic: the creation operation itself cannot be replaced by a subclass, a mock or a container, so creation policy cannot vary per context the way an overridable factory method allows.

Caching and interning factories introduce shared mutable state: lifetime, eviction and thread-safety become the type's responsibility, and callers may no longer assume two calls return distinct objects (value-based classes explicitly forbid relying on identity).

Call sites bind to one concrete static API, which makes substitution harder than constructor or interface injection: tests cannot swap the creation route without editing the call site or a global seam.

Every added route grows the API surface, and a factory name can hide real cost or side effects - a method called Load, Open or Connect performs I/O that a constructor call would never suggest, so the name must carry the semantics.

participants.responsibility: Declares the state and the invariants of the object and keeps its constructor(s) non-public whenever creation must flow through the named operations; may stay abstract and hide the concrete classes behind a base type or interface.

One class-level operation per construction intent; its name states what is being built (polar, probablePrime, fromPolar, NewClient, from_utf8). It validates inputs, converts units or encodings, may consult a cache, may choose a concrete subtype, and returns the least specific type that carries the contract.
Asks for the object by intent rather than by argument shape, and never constructs the type directly; it treats the returned type as the contract and does not depend on the concrete class.
Holds canonical, preconstructed or interned instances so that repeated requests can be served without allocation; defines identity semantics, thread-safety, boundedness and eviction.
The concrete class or subtype the factory actually instantiates - non-public, replaceable, and free to change between releases as long as the declared return type's contract holds.

use_cases: Value types whose construction routes collide in signature: Point::rectangular vs Point::polar, Duration.fromSeconds/fromMinutes/fromHours, Money.of(currency, amount), Temperature.fromFahrenheit.
Parsing and conversion entry points that can fail: Instant.parse, Path.of, String::from_utf8, TryFrom implementations, a TypeScript static from(input) that validates untrusted text.

Instance-controlled types: cached or interned instances (Boolean.valueOf, Symbol.for, canonical flyweight values, enum-like singletons) where repeated calls may legitimately return the identical object.

APIs that hide their implementation or select it from the arguments: List.of and Collections.unmodifiableList returning private classes, EnumSet choosing a representation by cardinality, Go constructors returning interfaces, Kotlin listOf returning a platform-specific implementation.

Ownership-sensitive creation: C++ factories returning std::unique_ptr/std::shared_ptr (and std::make_unique/make_shared as the library's own named constructors) or Rust constructors returning Box<dyn Trait> or Arc<Self>.

Constrained construction in domain models: Game.createSinglePlayerGame(), Order.draft(), Account.openedOn(date) - named routes that apply business rules so state combinations which must not happen cannot be constructed.

Java's JDK 9+ List.of, Set.of, and Map.of static factories create unmodifiable collections with input validation and compact representations; the named route communicates the mutability contract without exposing implementation classes.

Rust's TryFrom implementations and String::from_utf8 provide fallible, validated construction as Result<Self, Error>, making invalid conversions explicit instead of allowing lossy or partially initialized values.

Go's math/big package uses named NewInt, NewRat, and NewFloat functions where the package-level operation initializes pointer-backed numeric values and the package name supplies the context that keeps the API discoverable.
avoid_when: A single public constructor with self-describing parameter types is enough: the extra indirection buys nothing and costs discoverability (prefer constructors; use a factory only when the operation's semantics do not map to construction).
Construction has many optional steps or a growing set of parameters: use a Builder or Functional Options to add configuration surface instead of stacking more factory names.
Creation must be replaceable per context, injectable, or specialized by subclasses: use a polymorphic Factory Method or dependency injection rather than a static operation.

The language already expresses the intent at the call site - named/keyword arguments (Python, Ruby, Swift labels), C# object initializers and records, or a conversion protocol that already covers the case (From/Into, valueOf, Kernel conversion functions).
The only motive is brevity: create(a, b) forwarding to a constructor adds a second way to do one thing and hides the canonical creation route.
anti_patterns: Factory sprawl: a dozen near-synonymous create*/from*/with* methods per type, so the intended default is invisible and every caller picks a different route to the same object.
Flag-parameter factories: create(int type) or create(bool flag) switching internally and casting, which recreates constructor overloading at runtime instead of giving each route a name.
Static factories as hidden global state or service locator (Instance.getInstance() resolving configuration), making dependencies implicit and tests order-dependent.
Handing out mutable cached instances: callers share hidden state and one client's mutation corrupts another's object.
Pass-through factories that add no semantics (create(a, b) { return new T(a, b); }) - a second name for the constructor that only makes the creation path harder to find.
Signalling failure with null or a partially built object instead of an error/optional value, letting invalid state escape the type's invariant.
design_principles: Encapsulation of construction (information hiding): the constructor is an implementation detail, the named routes are the public API and the concrete class may stay invisible behind the declared return type.
Intention-revealing interfaces: a creation operation is named for the construction intent, not for the shape of its parameter list.
Invariants at the boundary of existence: validate where the object enters the system so that an existing instance is always valid (parse, don't validate; make illegal states unrepresentable).
Program to an interface, not an implementation: return the least specific type that carries the contract so hidden implementation classes stay replaceable.
Single responsibility per creation route and a single point of change for creation policy (validation, caching, representation and subtype choice).
best_practices: Name each operation after the construction intent (fromPolar, probablePrime, withCapacity, from_utf8) and follow the language's own conventions: of/valueOf/getInstance in Java, NewX in Go, new/with_*/from_* in Rust, from* in Kotlin/Python/Ruby, static make/from in Swift and TypeScript.

Keep constructors non-public whenever the factories enforce invariants, and document that the type is then not subclassable; keep at least one protected constructor when subclassing is part of the design (the C++ FAQ is explicit about this).

Return the least specific useful type - interfaces or base classes where implementations should stay hidden (List.of, EnumSet, factory functions returning Kotlin/Go interfaces), concrete types where the caller should choose the abstraction (accept interfaces, return structs in Go).
Decide and document identity semantics per route: say whether repeated calls may return a shared instance, require shared instances to be immutable, and make caches thread-safe and bounded.

Keep factories pure unless the name says otherwise: if an operation performs I/O, allocation of external resources or registration, let the name (open, load, connect) and the return type expose the failure mode.

Keep the factory set small and discoverable: one default route, creation documented in the type's class-level documentation, and no factory at all when a constructor or language-level named arguments already say what is meant.
